title: Mirror Neurons: Are there people who feel others' pain?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore synesthesia in its many forms (mirror touch, sound-color, color grapheme, word-taste, time-space), its likely genetic basis, and acquired synesthesia after blindness or brain injury. The episode then moves to mirror neurons, discovered in macaque monkeys by the University of Parma team (Rizzolatti, Gallese, Fogassi), their later observation in humans via epilepsy patients' electrodes, and their proposed role in empathy, learning, language, and autism. The hosts close with a philosophical aside about the "Fifth Revolution" in neuroscience and a brain-in-a-vat thought experiment. The episode ends with listener mail and T-shirt submission announcements.
topics: brain in a vat thought experiment

segments.title: Opening banter and synesthesia listener request
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the show. Chuck shares that he feels a shooting pain when he sees a leg or bone broken in sports, which leads into a discussion of mirror touch synesthesia.

segments.title: Types of synesthesia and their characteristics
segments.summary: The hosts define mirror touch synesthesia and sound-color synesthesia, noting that these experiences are real and not imagined, and that synesthesia is individual. They cite estimates that roughly one in a hundred or two hundred people have some degree of synesthesia, and discuss famous synesthetes including Nabokov, Liszt, and Duke Ellington.

segments.title: Color grapheme tests, word-taste and time-space synesthesia
segments.summary: The hosts describe the color grapheme test in which synesthetes quickly pick out fives among s's, and mention word-taste and touch pairings. They describe David Brang's time-space synesthesia study, in which a woman saw the year as a rotating ring around her body.

segments.title: Synesthesia and memory, and genetics
segments.summary: The hosts discuss research finding synesthetes recall more facts about events, with a study reporting an average of 123 facts versus 39. They then discuss the apparent genetic basis, including Sarah Jane Blakemore's finding that eleven relatives of a woman in her audience had synesthesia, and compare the number of genes involved to epidermolysis bullosa.

segments.title: Acquired synesthesia and pop culture references
segments.summary: The hosts distinguish developmental from acquired synesthesia, which can follow blindness, brain injury, or drug use. They reference the film Mask and the film Fantasia as examples of synesthesia-like imagery.

segments.title: Discovery of mirror neurons in macaque monkeys
segments.summary: The hosts recount how the University of Parma team of Rizzolatti, Gallese, and Fogassi discovered mirror neurons in macaque monkeys by accident. Neurons in the premotor cortex fired both when the monkey reached for a raisin and when a researcher reached for one.

segments.title: Mirror neurons in humans, empathy, and autism
segments.summary: The hosts describe how mirror neurons may underlie learning by observation, theory of mind, and empathy, and note that autism is associated with reduced mirror neuron activity. They report a UCLA study using electrodes in epilepsy patients, in which about eight percent of neurons fired both when grasping and when watching a grasp. They also mention that mirror neuron activity responds to sounds and sentences.

segments.title: Fifth Revolution, brain-in-a-vat, and language evolution
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh discuss mirror neurons as a possible basis for language evolution and the Fifth Revolution in science, following Copernicus, Darwin, Freud, and Watson and Crick. They raise Ramachandran's brain-in-a-vat thought experiment and reflect on the implications for the nature of reality.

segments.title: Further reading and related research
segments.summary: The hosts mention Richard Cytowic's books on synesthesia and the idea that synesthesia results from crossed wires in infant brains. They also mention a competing hypothesis that synesthetes pick up on real physical correspondences.

segments.title: Listener mail and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners, invite T-shirt submissions, and plug the show's Facebook and Twitter accounts and email address. The episode ends with a sign-off.
